about: Gap item 150 (Ram, 2026-11-20): a span that ties the Lapita, Hawaii, Rapa Nui and New Zealand drafts into one story.

spans.name: Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific
spans.date_display: c. 1000 BCE–1300 CE: from the Lapita voyages to the settlement of New Zealand
spans.description: The long settlement of the remote Pacific by seafaring peoples. Lapita voyagers reached Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, where Polynesian culture took shape; after a long pause their descendants sailed on to settle the islands from Hawaii to Rapa Nui and New Zealand.
spans.note: The Lapita settlers were the ancestors of the Polynesians rather than Polynesians themselves; the description says Polynesian culture took shape in Tonga and Samoa. The 'long pause' in West Polynesia lasted over a thousand years. The Chatham Islands were settled from New Zealand later (c. 1500), after this span's end.
spans.significance: Without metal tools, writing or navigational instruments, Pacific voyagers found and settled nearly every habitable island across a vast stretch of ocean. Their wayfinding by stars, swells and birds ranks among the great achievements of human exploration, and modern canoes such as Hōkūleʻa have revived it.

links.why: The Lapita crossing into Remote Oceania opened the settlement of the far Pacific.
Hawaii, the northern corner of the Polynesian triangle, was settled from East Polynesia.
Rapa Nui, the eastern corner of the triangle, was among the last islands reached.
New Zealand, the southern corner of the triangle, was the last large land mass settled.
